Build me a sparse, isolated winter settlement set in a broad snow-filled basin at warm, hazy sunset, with deep ivory snowdrifts, long blue-gray shadows, occasional falling snow, and wooded hills enclosing the scene. Place the main residential cluster along one side of a frozen lake or broad flooded plain: roughly three large, tall slab-shaped apartment blocks, each about ten stories, arranged loosely around short access roads and open courtyards rather than packed into a continuous street wall. Give them repetitive grid façades in weathered beige concrete, rows of small rectangular windows, and darker recessed balcony bands. Scatter about five smaller, boxy brick apartment buildings in front of and between the towers, generally four or five stories high, with snow-covered hipped or flat roofs, chimneys, antennas, and a few warmly lit windows. Run a narrow cracked asphalt road past the buildings, bend it around the courtyards, and continue it beside the lake before carrying it across the frozen water on a long, straight, low bridge supported by simple piers. Edge parts of the lakeside road and open ground with segmented decorative concrete fencing. Keep the central landscape largely undeveloped: rolling, wind-sculpted snowbanks, shallow gullies, exposed patches of dark road or water, scattered shrubs, and a few small frozen pools or irregular black openings in the ice. Add several isolated cottages or utility-like brick structures among the snow-covered slopes and woods, including a weathered two-story masonry house with a chimney, rooftop antennas, and smoke rising. Populate the terrain organically with dense stands of snow-laden birch and pine near the settlement, sparser leafless trees and twisted bushes across the open mounds, and thicker evergreen forests climbing the surrounding hills. Let the outer boundary dissolve into uneven snowy ridges, forested mountains, and the frozen lake, keeping the overall composition quiet, spacious, weathered, and only lightly inhabited.

Place the main residential cluster along one side of a frozen lake or broad flooded plain: roughly three large, tall slab-shaped apartment blocks, each about ten stories, arranged loosely around short access roads and open courtyards rather than packed into a continuous street wall. Give them repetitive grid façades in weathered beige concrete, rows of small rectangular windows, and darker recessed balcony bands. Scatter about five smaller, boxy brick apartment buildings in front of and between the towers, generally four or five stories high, with snow-covered hipped or flat roofs, chimneys, antennas, and a few warmly lit windows. Run a narrow cracked asphalt road past the buildings, bend it around the courtyards, and continue it beside the lake before carrying it across the frozen water on a long, straight, low bridge supported by simple piers. Edge parts of the lakeside road and open ground with segmented decorative concrete fencing. Keep the central landscape largely undeveloped: rolling, wind-sculpted snowbanks, shallow gullies, exposed patches of dark road or water, scattered shrubs, and a few small frozen pools or irregular black openings in the ice. Add several isolated cottages or utility-like brick structures among the snow-covered slopes and woods, including a weathered two-story masonry house with a chimney, rooftop antennas, and smoke rising. Populate the terrain organically with dense stands of snow-laden birch and pine near the settlement, sparser leafless trees and twisted bushes across the open mounds, and thicker evergreen forests climbing the surrounding hills. Let the outer boundary dissolve into uneven snowy ridges, forested mountains, and the frozen lake, keeping the overall composition quiet, spacious, weathered, and only lightly inhabited.
